Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥 Our philosophy A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity. To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally. On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers. Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases! See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards. Composable Images Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along! Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve. As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot. TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images Types Beyond Decisions We’re introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support. We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers). Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box Size does matter, apparently 💅 We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod. We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length Opt-in to help us We love the community’s desire to help make models better! blogs.content: How Jack & Jill Cut Candidate Screening Costs By 88% With Jev - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Case Study Case Study ')"> How Jack & Jill Cut Candidate Screening Costs By 88% With Jev Oct 7, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 We saved ~half a million dollars last week with Jev. And our products got much better at the same time. Matthew Wilson, Co-founder/CEO @ Jack & Jill View post on LinkedIn Background Jack & Jill is a talent marketplace brokered by AI agents. Jack is a career agent for top professionals and Jill is an agent for hiring teams. When Jack and Jill agree there is a mutual match, they introduce the candidate and the company directly, skipping the application altogether. To date, they’ve worked with over 5,000 companies and more than 400,000 professionals working in startups - and raised a total of $60M in the process. Within 10 days of their first test, Jack & Jill had fully rolled out Jev in production - replacing Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite for 100% of calls for a key stage in their candidate matching pipeline. Compared to Gemini, Jev maintained the same level of accuracy, with 88% lower cost and roughly 50% faster task completion time. Cost savings are projected to be $500K per year - and more importantly, new use cases have been unlocked across the product, such as showing candidates matched jobs immediately after signup. Impact Result Details ↓ $500K/year Absolute projected savings ↓ 88% cost BEFORE | $0.755 with Google Gemini AFTER | $0.092 with TypeSafe Jev Cost per 1,000 candidates scored 2x speed BEFORE | 20.3 sec AFTER | 10.3 sec Median time to screen each candidate No loss in quality BEFORE | 93.9% Baseline AFTER | 94.6% Candidates requested by hiring managers The challenge: expensive to screen a large volume of candidates with Gemini Before Jev Candidate pool. Every day, 6,000 candidates for every open role are pulled from the database Initial scoring. A low-cost model (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) scores each candidate and creates a shortlist of the top 2,000 candidates Close review. A higher-power model assesses the top 2,000 candidates, ending with a list of a few hundred candidates for the hiring manager Even with a “low-cost” model like Gemini Flash Lite, costs were adding up fast, due to the "Initial scoring" step that assessed 6,000 candidates for every open role. Results with Jev: Similar quality to Gemini at 88% lower cost With Jev Before switching, Jack & Jill tested both Gemini and Jev models on 150 live roles, and the same candidates for each role. For each role, they included: every past “winner”: a candidate a hiring manager later asked to meet a sample of remaining candidates (weighted to accurately represent the original 6,000 candidates retrieved for each role) The test counted how many winners each model kept on the shortlist. For example, a score of 95% means that for every 100 candidates that the hiring manager asked to be introduced to, the model correctly kept 95 of them in its shortlist. Ultimately, Jack & Jill found that Jev was able to maintain similar quality to Gemini, with 88% lower cost and half the median time to complete scoring. Overall, the team expects to save more than $500K based on projected volumes over the next 12 months. Jev’s score of 0.933 means it ranked the winner higher in approximately 93.3% of those pairings, compared with 92.4% for Gemini — aligning better with the recorded hiring manager selections. blogs.content: Insights How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 In-house legal teams face a steady stream of work that varies in urgency, complexity, and the judgment required. AI can accelerate first drafts and other preparatory work, giving lawyers more room to focus on decisions that require their deep knowledge of the business. That raises an important question for legal leaders: Which work should the team take on vs. hand off to AI, and where can its lawyers add the most value? At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Silv Roest, Group Chief Legal, Corporate Affairs, and Sustainability Officer at The Warehouse Group; Andrew Chivers, Regional General Counsel, APAC at Brambles Limited; and Georgette Apostolopoulos, General Counsel at The Star shared what they’re learning as AI becomes part of their teams’ day-to-day work. Their examples offer practical lessons for using AI to change how legal teams work, beyond accelerating individual tasks. Change How the Work is Divided At The Warehouse Group, one of the largest retailing groups in New Zealand, Roest is looking at how a four-lawyer team spends its time. First drafts, summaries, and issue tables are necessary work, but they can make it difficult to reach the questions that need the team’s judgment and knowledge of the business. That makes the division of work a useful place to start. Watch Video Apostolopoulos faced a different capacity challenge at The Star, one of Australia’s leading integrated resort companies. After the legal team downsized, it no longer had an in-house litigator to run an anti-discrimination matter. Her team used AI to help prepare the evidence before asking outside firms for quotes. By preparing the evidence in-house, the team could ask firms to price the work that remained, giving it a way to manage outside counsel costs. Watch Video Both examples start by breaking work into its component steps. Legal leaders can then identify what AI can help prepare, where their lawyers need to apply judgment, and when outside counsel’s expertise is needed. That gives a lean team a clearer way to allocate its time and scope external work. Make Existing Knowledge Easier to Use For a legal team supporting a global business, even a familiar question can take time to answer when the relevant guidance sits across different policies and jurisdictions. Global supply chain logistics company Brambles has 24 lawyers working across 60 countries. Chivers described how his team brought its policies together in an agent that people can query, reducing the need to search through documents each time a question comes in. Watch Video The example offers a useful starting point for teams with knowledge spread across many documents: look for questions that come up repeatedly and require lawyers to consult the same sources. Making those sources easier to use can help the team respond more quickly, while lawyers still assess how the guidance applies to the particular situation. Help Lawyers Evaluate AI Output Making information easier to access also changes the skills lawyers need to practice. Chivers noted that junior lawyers may be comfortable using AI while still developing the legal knowledge needed to challenge its answers. Familiarity with the tool is useful; the ability to spot a missing fact, weak inference, or incorrect conclusion takes training. Watch Video That training can happen in the course of real work. When reviewing an AI-assisted draft, a supervising lawyer can ask a junior colleague what they checked, where the answer came from, and why they agree with it. The discussion helps the junior lawyer develop judgment alongside their ability to use the tool. blogs.content: Product Making Harvey the Orchestration Layer for Legal Work Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents. by Harvey Team • Oct 15, 2026 Today, we’re launching Legal Work Orchestration , a new way to organize and manage legal matters in Harvey. It connects the phases, tasks, people, and review points within a matter so that agents can execute defined tasks, lawyers can review their work at designated gates, and everyone involved can see what needs to happen next. Watch Video Much of legal work follows a repeatable process. An M&A transaction, for example, moves through familiar phases, tasks, and review points. But the process itself often has to be reconstructed for every new matter from a checklist, a previous deal, or the knowledge of the people who have done it before. AI agents can already complete many individual steps within that process. What they often lack is the structure around the task: where it fits in the matter, which documents and instructions apply, who should review the output, and what happens next. Lawyers still have to provide that context, move the work between people and systems, and track its progress. Legal Work Orchestration brings that structure into Harvey, allowing lawyers and agents to work through a matter together in one place. How Legal Orchestration Works The same structure can support any matter or project a team runs more than once, from an M&A transaction to a quarterly compliance review. Legal Work Orchestration captures that process in a reusable template, carries the relevant context into each task, and coordinates reviews and next steps. Capture the Process in a Reusable Template Templates capture how your organization runs a recurring type of work. When an associate opens a new buy-side acquisition, the Space can already contain the relevant phases, tasks, playbooks, agents, collaborators, and review gates. Innovation and knowledge teams can define that structure once, helping teams follow a consistent process across matters without rebuilding it from scratch. Give Every Task the Context it Needs Each task includes its scope, inputs, and reviewer. An agent assigned a change-of-control review can therefore analyze the relevant contracts and produce a consent matrix without the lawyer having to assemble a new prompt and briefing for that step. Tasks can also be assigned to another lawyer or shared with the client while retaining the relevant matter context. The work no longer depends on one person manually carrying information from one step to the next. Keep Reviews and Next Steps Moving When the agent completes the review, Harvey notifies the designated partner that the consent matrix is ready. Once the partner approves it, the task is completed and the next step can begin. Updates can also be made from email. A lawyer can ask Harvey in a reply to close a task or begin the next one, while the Space maintains a current view of the matter’s progress. Partners can see where the work stands without asking an associate to reconstruct the status from email and separate checklists. The Future of Legal Work Orchestration Before the release of Harvey II in August, every step delegated to Harvey required a lawyer to gather the documents, write the instructions, and move the output to wherever it needed to go next. Legal Work Orchestration reduces that overhead by giving each task its inputs, instructions, and reviewer in advance. Today, lawyers still actively prompt the majority of steps in a legal workflow. We expect that balance to change rapidly. Over the next six months, we expect agents to take on an additional 20% of workflow steps. Within a year, we expect that share to triple. blogs.content: Insights Building a Frontier In-House Organization How legal teams are transforming their departments with Harvey to better serve the enterprise and help the business move faster. by Matt Zerweck and Gabe Pereyra • Oct 13, 2026 Satya Nadella describes the frontier firm as a company built around intelligence on demand, where people and agents work side by side. Inside most companies, the legal department is where that shift arrives first. For the general counsels we work with, the question used to be how to get lawyers to use AI. Now it’s how to run the department on it. Behind that shift are four challenges we hear from in-house teams: Legal as the bottleneck. Lawyers spend too much time on work that doesn’t need legal judgment, instead of working at the top of their license. Rising volume, flat headcount. Demand for Legal grows with the business but headcount and budgets do not. Reactive instead of proactive. Regulatory change and contract risk surface late, when they’re already problems. No portfolio visibility. Contract history, obligations, and outside matters are scattered across systems, inboxes, and law firms. None of these problems stay in one lane. A single contract can be a bottleneck, a capacity problem, and a visibility gap at once. And when requests queue up and the business can’t see where they stand, employees bypass Legal and take legal questions to general-purpose AI tools, outside Legal’s controls. Banning that doesn't work. The frontier move is to give the business a better place to ask, with Legal in control of the answers. The Platform for a Frontier Legal Department Figure 1. The legal department of a frontier firm with everything in one place. We’re building Harvey as one platform for the business, its legal team, and outside counsel. It connects every request, contract, and matter with the documents, conversations, and context behind it. That knowledge, including the department’s policies, prior decisions, and outcomes, is codified in one legal brain that people and agents draw on as they work. Legal decides what agents can handle and where people should make the call. Legal puts that knowledge to work across requests, contracts, and matters. It sets what agents can handle, where people make the call, and when to involve outside counsel. Past matters, outcomes, and invoice data help Legal choose the right firm for the work. Requests come in and follow-up questions, updates, and completed work go back through the channels the business already uses. Each outcome adds to the department’s knowledge, informing the next decision. Figure 2. The platform architecture. Connected systems feed a shared model of the department’s work, with source permissions preserved. Harvey’s products and agents draw on that same model. If a sales lead asks whether a customer deal can include a new AI-use clause, Harvey can pull up the original request, the department’s position on AI clauses, the terms the company has agreed to before, and the EU rules that apply, all in one answer. We've built that connectivity with partners over several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft Azure and works inside Microsoft 365 , from Word to Copilot Cowork. It connects to LexisNexis for primary law, to Docusign and Ironclad for contract workflows, and through the Connector Library to the rest of the systems the department already uses. Resolve Requests Wherever the Business Works Intake extends the department’s legal front door across email, chat, and business systems, including Outlook, Gmail, Slack, Teams, Jira, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. Harvey gathers context, then routes and assigns work by type, risk, and department. Agents and lawyers send follow-up questions, updates, and completed work back through the same channels. Figure 3. As CEO and Managing Partner, Lydia oversees the firm's six offices in Atlantic Canada, more than 250 lawyers, and over 350 staff on any given day. As Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer and Partner, Paul co-chairs the firm's AI and Technology Steering Committee, drives strategy and innovation across the firm, and is now Managing Director of Stewart McKelvey’s newest venture: the Fortified Firm. Eleven years ago, the two of them made the case to the firm's partnership board for something no one at Stewart McKelvey had done before: a dedicated practice innovation function. Its job was to systematically improve how the firm practiced law, covering everything from process and pricing to technology and profitability. They made that call years before generative AI existed, which is largely why the firm was ready to move fast once AI arrived to the business of law in a substantive way. Two different starting points, one shared instinct Lydia's path to leadership ran through in-house roles first. Those years gave her an early look at how good businesses are run, rather than just the legal work layered on top of them. Sitting on the client side meant understanding different law firms' value for herself, and taking on project work that stretched beyond legal advice into the operational side of the business. "They always let me do a little bit more than just the law," she says. "And I enjoyed that quite a bit." She became CEO and Managing Partner in August 2015, and has since been balancing the collegiality of a partnership alongside the discipline of running Atlantic Canada’s largest law firm. Early on, she pushed back when a senior partner insisted the firm was a partnership, not a business, telling him they were "professionals in a big business." This ability to see what's working ‘under the hood’ is what took her from evaluating outside counsel to running a substantial business. Paul came to law with a background in finance and technology. "I just started to look at opportunities to systematize, improve processes, solve problems," he says, recalling his first summer at work. Lydia noticed early. "Paul was the young lawyer you'd have someone pitch a virtual data room to for 50,000 US dollars," she says, "and he'd come in on a Monday and say, if you don't mind, I spent 18 dollars on a license, and here's a secure data room we can use. He'd solve the problem, but he'd also build something everyone else at the firm could use." By his fifth or sixth year practicing, Paul took a secondment to work on technology projects, and a trip to a legal conference in Chicago sharpened his sense of urgency. "I just couldn't believe what some of the conversations about profitability and leverage and pricing were, things we just weren't exploring at that point," he says. He came back and, in the fall of 2015, not long after Lydia became CEO, the two of them flew to St. John's to pitch creating a practice innovation role to the partnership board. Paul left his practice to become the firm's first Practice Innovation Partner, building out document automation, process mapping, and checklists. "It wasn't a hard sell," Lydia says. "Paul said he wanted to devote 100 percent of his time to the firm, and it just mushroomed from there." Today, he's known at Legora for tackling the problems with no obvious owner, the unglamorous work that falls between the cracks but can make or break a company as it scales. Finding his way to Legora Oskar’s career started at EY, where he trained as an auditor before realizing that his real interest was in data. That led him to a Swedish energy startup, where he worked on building data infrastructure, and eventually into backend development. But Oskar's move to Legora was different. It wasn’t simply the role that convinced him to make the jump. It was the people and the way they thought. “It didn’t feel like a traditional interview. I was actually working on a coding problem, and it led to a really interesting discussion and sharing of ideas within the team. I knew after that meeting I had to be involved in building this company, and work alongside people who think the same way as me.” Being surrounded by people who are willing to question how things are done and figure things out together has continued to be a big focus when hiring new members of Oskar’s team as they scale. Scaling without losing the culture Oskar’s role has changed significantly over time as the company has grown. The engineering team has grown with it, but the culture that brought people together early on has remained remarkably consistent, with an emphasis on high standards, a willingness to take ownership and a shared appetite for constantly building. blogs.content: Company Harvey to Open Tokyo Office by Harvey Team • Oct 12, 2026 Harvey will open an office in Tokyo in early 2027, deepening our commitment to supporting law firms and in-house legal teams in Japan. Trust is earned over time through close collaboration and consistent support. As we grow in Japan, we are investing in a local presence to build lasting relationships, listen to our customers, and ensure their needs guide how we continue to build and grow here. Our Tokyo office will support our growing customer base in Japan and deepen relationships with law firms including Mori Hamada & Matsumoto and Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu, and in-house legal teams, including Mitsubishi Corporation. A local presence will help us work more closely with these teams and strengthen the support we provide. We are also building Harvey to better support work in Japanese and reflect the needs of legal professionals in Japan. This includes our partnership with Legalscape for Japanese legal research. Working with local experts and listening to customer feedback will help guide how we develop our product and support its use. “Japan is a critical market for legal and home to many exceptional law firms and companies. With the government investing in AI acceleration country-wide, there’s no better time to bring Harvey to Tokyo,” said Winston Weinberg, Harvey’s Chief Executive Officer. “Having a team in Japan will help us better understand the needs of legal professionals in Japan and make their experience central to how we build and grow here.” Koji Toshima, Partner and CFO, Mori Hamada & Matsumoto, said, “Since establishing our partnership with Harvey in 2024, we have worked closely together to explore how AI can enhance the quality and efficiency of legal services in Japan. Harvey’s decision to open a Tokyo office is a very welcome and significant milestone, demonstrating its strong commitment to the Japanese legal market. Building on our collaboration to date, including our recent support in bringing about the partnership between Harvey and Legalscape, we look forward to further strengthening our collaboration with Harvey to advance the development of innovative AI solutions tailored to the needs of Japanese legal practice and deliver even greater value to our clients in Japan and around the world.” Tokyo will expand Harvey’s existing presence across Asia-Pacific, alongside our teams in Sydney, Singapore, and Bengaluru. blogs.content: Insights Vendor Contract Management Starts With Legal Setting the Standard Procurement owns the supplier relationship. Legal owns whether the terms hold. Here's how legal sets the standard once and reviews only the exceptions. by Harvey Team • Oct 9, 2026 Vendor contract management is the process of creating, negotiating, and monitoring supplier agreements, also called vendor contracts, so the organization gets the value it pays for while managing risk. In most organizations, Procurement owns the supplier relationship, spend management, and renewal timelines, and Legal owns whether the terms survive a regulator, an incident, or an audit. Those responsibilities are distinct, but they intersect every time a supplier agreement enters the review process. That overlap explains a common problem: agreements reach Legal too late, with key terms already negotiated, or too early, requiring attorney time for matters Procurement could have handled. As contract volume grows, neither pattern scales. A more scalable approach starts by separating routine reviews from true exceptions. With Harvey, Legal encodes its positions once in a Playbook, the business runs a first pass against that standard, and only agreements that fall outside approved positions escalate to counsel. This article covers review and escalation before signature, and it answers one question: which supplier agreements Legal reviews and which the business runs itself. Building the playbook and benchmarking incoming paper against it clause by clause are separate jobs. To see how teams use Spaces for collaboration beyond supplier review, start with Harvey's guide to legal collaboration . Commitments that arise after signature are a different job again: contract obligation management. What Legal Reviews in a Supplier Agreement Every supplier agreement contains two kinds of provisions: commercial terms and risk allocation. Procurement evaluates and negotiates the commercial side, such as pricing, service levels, delivery schedules, usage rights, and commercial commitments. These matters determine whether a supplier relationship makes business sense. Legal focuses on the second kind. Vendor contract review, sometimes called third-party contract review, covers the risk-allocation provisions that need legal judgment beyond Procurement's commercial read: Data processing terms Breach notification windows Subcontractor disclosure requirements Audit rights Indemnity obligations Termination rights Flow-down obligations Regulatory compliance commitments These clauses determine how responsibility is shared when something goes wrong and whether the organization can meet its own obligations to regulators, customers, and business partners. The security stakes are measurable: SecurityScorecard's 2025 Global Third-Party Breach Report found that 35.5% of breaches in 2024 were third-party related. None of this replaces the contract lifecycle management (CLM) system already in use. The CLM remains the system of record for routing, approvals, execution, and storage. Harvey's integration with Icertis works inside that process: users extract terms, analyze them against Playbooks, and determine the level of risk and review required without leaving the CLM. The distinction becomes clearer when different functions look at the same agreement: Function The question it answers Procurement Should we buy from this supplier, at what price, on what terms? Third-party risk management Can this supplier be relied on operationally and financially? Legal contract review Do the terms hold up against a regulator, an incident, or an audit? Each function reads the same document against a different standard. Legal's attention narrows to the provisions that create regulatory, contractual, or compliance exposure, and that's where the reading gets hardest. blogs.content: Insights Contract Obligation Management Has to Follow the Contract as it Changes See how legal teams read renewal dates, notice periods, and covenants out of signed agreements so the obligation register matches the contract. by Harvey Team • Oct 8, 2026 A supply agreement required 90 days' written notice before renewal if either party intended not to renew. The obligation register recorded the renewal date, but not the obligation inside the clause: the notice period began 90 days earlier. By the time the renewal date arrived, the opportunity to act had already passed. Contract obligation management is the work of tracking what a signed agreement requires of each party, when each requirement comes due, and what triggers it. The trouble starts when a register records someone's summary of a clause, the way that supply agreement's register recorded only the renewal date. Harvey reads the executed contract and identifies what is owed, what triggers the obligation, and what conditions affect it, so the register reflects what the clause requires. This article covers what happens after signature, and it focuses on reading obligations rather than storing contracts. If you're looking for where agreements live and move, start with contract lifecycle management . For the wider in-house process around them, see in-house contract management . Three adjacent disciplines get discussed together even though they answer different questions: Discipline The question it answers Contract lifecycle management Where is the agreement, and what stage is it in? Contract obligation management What did we commit to, and when does it come due? Regulatory obligation mapping What do the rules require of us, independent of any contract? Why the Obligation Register Goes Stale World Commerce & Contracting's August 2025 study found an average value erosion of 8.6% from poor contract management. An obligation register is often populated once, when the agreement is signed, based on the understanding of the person reviewing the contract at that point. From then on, the register stays static while the contract continues to evolve, and three gaps begin to emerge: Reviewers frequently summarize obligations rather than analyzing them in detail. A reviewer may record a renewal date without capturing the notice requirement that comes before it. Obligations are often event-driven rather than calendar-driven. An obligation may depend on a business event, a regulatory filing, a financial threshold, or another condition that triggers action only when circumstances change. Amendments alter the underlying agreement. New language can modify deadlines, add reporting requirements, or change existing commitments. If nobody analyzes those amendments and reflects them in the obligation register, the register quickly becomes outdated. Covenant tracking in credit agreements shows how the three gaps compound. A lender may require financial statements within a set number of days after quarter-end, compliance certificates tied to those statements, and notice obligations triggered by material events. None of those commitments exists in isolation, since each depends on timing, definitions, and relationships elsewhere in the agreement. A summary misses the dependencies, an event-driven notice never reaches a calendar, and one amended definition can move all three. Each gap traces back to a one-time reading at intake. Harvey II lets agents inherit the context of the matter or project they open in. For an in-house deal, that includes the counterparty, whose paper the team is on, and the positions the team has taken before. An agent working an amendment starts from that context, so the reading carries forward with the contract. What Reading an Obligation Produces An obligation isn't a single field. blogs.content: Insights AI Fluency Is Legal Education's New Differentiator by Keith Enright • Oct 8, 2026 The team at Harvey is proud to work with more than 100 law schools globally. As AI transforms the business and practice of law, we see an opportunity and an obligation to help educators prepare the next generation of lawyers. Employers increasingly expect graduates to use AI in practice, while educators rightly insist that students develop independent judgment and analytical skills. These aims belong together: using AI well requires students to question its output, test its limits, and decide when to set it aside. That fluency takes guided practice alongside a rigorous legal education. Working hand in hand with educators, we aim to help students build the skills necessary for today’s and tomorrow's legal industry. The Need for Adaptation is Evident For most of my career, I’ve worked closely with senior legal leaders at the intersection of technology and the delivery of legal work. We’ve talked about the future of the profession, the challenges and opportunities we are facing, and how technology can help lawyers thrive and deliver more client value. There has always been discussion of how the profession must adapt to new technology, but the urgency and prominence of these issues has accelerated noticeably in the last 12 months. This shift has been coupled with a growing recognition of the need for incoming lawyers who can use AI thoughtfully and responsibly from their first day. Many firms are investing heavily in AI and anticipate that digitally native graduates will arrive fluent and excited to use these tools. But that influx of AI-fluent talent is taking longer to deliver than many presumed. Even when first-years show up ready to work in an AI-enabled practice, many are still inexperienced with the leading tools, as they haven’t yet had sufficient experience using them to deliver legal work. In these circumstances, the burden of AI training is increasingly shifted to employers, delaying the ability of young lawyers to deliver value on client work and forcing tenured employees to become trainers. Increasing law student exposure to AI during legal education benefits future associates by making them more marketable to employers of all kinds and more immediately productive. It benefits employers when new hires deliver more value more quickly. And it benefits the schools themselves by strengthening their relationships with potential employers, and giving prospective students more confidence in their post-graduation prospects. AI fluency means something specific here. That's a professional skill, and like every professional skill, it takes practice. Students who get reps practicing how to work with AI in school will be able to work more effectively and efficiently when they start their legal careers. The core tension is easy to state. The profession's expectations of a first-year lawyer are changing more rapidly than law schools are adapting their curricula and policies. blogs.content: Technical Building Harvey’s MCP Policy Engine Runtime controls add another layer of protection for Harvey and its customers by governing tool access, information flow, and agent actions beyond the initial connector review. by Suha Sabi Hussain , Divya Sudhakar , and Nick Gonella • Oct 7, 2026 Legal teams work across research platforms, document management systems, and communication tools. Connecting Harvey Agents to those systems gives them more context and more ways to help users complete work. It also creates a security challenge: tools can change after initial review, return malicious instructions, or be exploited in ways that expose sensitive information. As we rebuilt our Connector Library , we built a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Policy Engine to govern how agents use partner MCP tools throughout a workflow. Prompt injection remains an open problem in AI security, so our approach draws on security research and uses multiple architectural controls to reduce the likelihood and impact of misuse. Our design draws inspiration from Sondera , Progent , ETDI , and CaMeL , which explore enforcing policies outside the model, limiting tool privileges, and controlling information flow. These ideas inform the boundaries we enforce as agents use partner MCP tools. In this post, we explain how the controls work, what we’ve learned, and where we’re continuing to improve. Why MCP Integrations Need Runtime Controls MCP expands what agents can do through a common, reusable standard for discovering tools, accessing data, and acting across services. It also expands the attack surface: bringing externally supplied tool definitions, content, and interaction requests into an agent’s workflow while also increasing existing supply chain risk. These risks have surfaced in multiple real attack campaigns and disclosed vulnerabilities . Our approach to MCP security starts with four considerations: MCP can grant individual servers power over the workflow. Alongside exposing tools that access data and act across services, servers can, where supported, ask clients to invoke models or collect information from users. This bidirectional design requires explicit limits on what servers can request and what clients will allow. Risk compounds across tools. We are concerned about the “lethal trifecta” : combining access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and external communication can result in impactful prompt injection leading to data exfiltration. MCP makes these capabilities both easy to combine and hard to control across independently evolving integrations. Even a trusted tool can return attacker-controlled content that redirects subsequent calls to retrieve and disclose sensitive information. Security depends on implementation. The NSA describes MCP’s security posture as “uneven and highly dependent on implementation discipline rather than protocol guarantees.” Each server, client, and host must enforce permissions, validate inputs, and handle consent. The protocol keeps evolving. New specifications can close existing gaps while introducing capabilities with novel risks . Our policy engine targets two particularly persistent threats that are harder to mitigate using existing tools. Both can exploit the lethal trifecta to exfiltrate sensitive data. In a tool poisoning attack , malicious instructions embedded in a tool's definition redirect the agent's behavior. In a rug-pull attack, a server introduces malicious changes after it has been approved, exploiting the trust placed in a previously reviewed tool. From Weeks of Associate Time to a Single Review-and-Approve Loop Drafting a motion to dismiss is one of the most time-intensive tasks in early-stage litigation. Typically, an associate has to read the complaint, spot viable grounds for dismissal, research each ground in the right jurisdiction, check for adverse authority, and draft 20–30 pages of intensely researched arguments. This multi-step process commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work. The new MTD workflow streamlines this entire process — just upload the complaint, approve the strategy, review the research brief, and watch Harvey prepare your first draft. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. blogs.content: KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Perspectives KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen Category Perspectives published Oct 13, 2026 author Janusch Krasberg Anfang 2026 arbeiteten rund 3.000 Juristinnen und Juristen in Deutschland mit Legora. Bei der Eröffnung des Münchner Büros Ende September waren es bereits mehr als 13.000. Besonders stark wächst die Nutzung in Rechtsabteilungen: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Nutzenden seit Januar verachtfacht. Deutschland hat den Ruf, neue Technologien eher zögerlich aufzugreifen. Bei KI zeichnet sich ein anderes Bild ab: Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen setzen die Technologie mit bemerkenswertem Tempo ein. Für den deutschen Markt reicht es nicht, KI ins Deutsche zu übersetzen. Sie muss auf das deutsche Recht und die Arbeitsweise juristischer Teams ausgerichtet sein. In unseren Gesprächen mit Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz verändern sich die Fragen. In ersten Tests von KI-Lösungen für den Rechtsbereich ging es vor allem darum, wie verlässlich KI bei Recherche, Analyse und Entwürfen unterstützt. Inzwischen beschäftigen sich die Teams zunehmend mit der Auswahl eines passenden Anbieters, der Einführung im Team und der Einbindung in bestehende Arbeitsabläufe. Bei der Auswahl einer passenden Lösung zeigt sich in intensiven Pilotphasen, wie gut sie zum eigenen Arbeitsalltag passt. Teams bringen dafür ihre vorhandenen Unterlagen, ihr Wissen und ihre internen Vorgaben ein. Entscheidend ist, wie gut Legora diese Informationen nutzbar macht und sich an die Arbeitsweise des jeweiligen Teams anpasst: wie Ergebnisse aufbereitet werden, wie sie in die weitere Beratung einfließen und wie Kolleginnen und Kollegen damit zusammenarbeiten. Was deutsche juristische Arbeit von KI verlangt Wer Rechts-KI in Deutschland einführt, trifft auf konkrete fachliche Anforderungen. Das beginnt bei der Sprache. Eine juristische Stellungnahme auf Deutsch muss Fachbegriffe präzise verwenden, die relevante Fragestellung erfassen und eine nachvollziehbare Argumentation enthalten. Bei grenzüberschreitenden Mandaten kommen unterschiedliche Arbeitssprachen hinzu. Ein englischsprachiger Vertrag kann die Grundlage für eine deutsche Stellungnahme bilden, die anschließend mit einem internationalen Team abgestimmt wird. Eigene Vertragsmuster und frühere Stellungnahmen ermöglichen es Teams, Entwürfe in Legora an den fachlichen und sprachlichen Standards ihrer Organisation auszurichten. Ebenso entscheidend sind die Rechtsquellen. Gesetze, Rechtsprechung und Kommentarliteratur bilden zusammen mit dem Wissen der jeweiligen Organisation die Grundlage juristischer Arbeit. Real-world knowledge work introduces distinct requirements: models must digest fragmented source files under concrete objectives and tight delivery constraints, structure specialized knowledge into cohesive analysis, and maintain domain rigor across the full execution lifecycle. Not just what the output looks like, but what happens around it before anyone trusts it. A coding agent can write code that compiles, runs, and looks clean, and still be wrong in ways that only show up later. Engineers learned not to judge the AI's output alone, but the system built around it: the tests, reviews, and guardrails that catch problems before they ship. There's a name for that system now. Software teams call it the harness, and building it well is harness engineering. What harness engineering is At a high level, an AI agent system can be understood as a model (or set of models), while everything around it is the harness. Writing on Martin Fowler's site, Thoughtworks' Birgitta Böckeler defines the harness as the instructions, tools, context, and checks that decide how the model behaves and how it catches itself when it's wrong. Harness engineering is the process of building and improving everything that defines how the model behaves and how it arrives at a reliable and accurate output. OpenAI's engineering team learned this by building an internal product with no hand-written code . Their takeaway: humans steer, agents execute. Their hardest problems weren’t about the model, they were about the harness. Böckeler organizes the harness into two kinds of controls: guides and sensors . Guides steer the AI before it acts, so it starts in the right place. Sensors check it after, so it can detect its own mistakes before you see them. The human's job isn't just to write clever prompts. It's to notice when the system makes the same mistake twice, then fix the guide or the sensor so it stops. A guide can be as simple as a project instruction. Building sensors that detect errors is where a purpose-built legal AI tool earns its place in an attorney’s tech stack. blogs.author: Shadi
blogs.description: A conversation with Jerry Levine (Leah), Colin Levy (Malbek) and Rich Robinson (Epiq) Change management is an essential part of getting buy-in and ROI from legal technology investments. The gap between promise and outcome is already showing up in the numbers: legal AI adoption reached 78% in 2026, up from just 23% in 2023, yet […] The post How Much of the Change Management Journey Does the Vendor Own? appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: A conversation with Jerry Levine (Leah), Colin Levy (Malbek) and Rich Robinson (Epiq) Change management is an essential part of getting buy-in and ROI from legal technology investments. The gap between promise and outcome is already showing up in the numbers: legal AI adoption reached 78% in 2026 , up from just 23% in 2023, yet actual time savings from these tools have averaged 18.3% against a median vendor projection of 41% , according to research from the Legal Stack. Clearly, more change management is needed to support ROI expectations. But where does “vendor support” end and organizational change management begin? What is it reasonable for buyers to expect from a vendor, and what requires wider, enterprise change? We put the questions to three leaders who sit in different seats – a CLM platform, an e-discovery managed-services provider, and a legal AI company – and let them talk it through. What follows is an edited version of that conversation. No vendor can own transformation on behalf of the customer RICH ROBINSON (Epiq): I think the best vendors help organizations navigate change. What they can’t do is own transformation on behalf of the customer. We can provide the methodology, training, coaching, governance, and measurement. The organization still has to bring the leadership, accountability, and willingness to work differently. In my experience, the implementations that hold up are the ones where both sides share ownership of the journey. JERRY LEVINE (Leah): That’s a useful distinction to draw out, because my role isn’t what Rich just described, and I think buyers often assume every vendor is offering some version of it. Someone in a role like Rich’s delivers a change management program as part of what Epiq delivers. My role is different. I get adoption questions constantly, usually from a GC asking how to get people using the tool. I’ll talk it through with them. What I offer is guidance. You need someone internally, often externally too, who owns that work. COLIN LEVY (Malbek): I’d put myself closer to Jerry on that spectrum than to Rich. Malbek is a software vendor, not a managed-services business. Buyers want a partner now, not just a system. In my experience, that shows up as co-building the product with the customer, and staying in the relationship well past the sale. None of that is change management. It’s what separates a good vendor from one who shows up for the sale and disappears. If neither side has the resources, bring in a third party RICH: That’s why I think it’s important that whoever is running the selection and deployment process goes in with eyes open. You have to be honest about your own resources and about your vendor’s resources. Change management is critical to adoption. If neither side has the acumen or the bandwidth for it, my advice is to hire a third-party implementation partner rather than hope the gap closes on its own. JERRY: That gap is where things fall apart in practice. A customer comes back and asks how to get adoption going, and the honest answer depends on questions that often don’t have consistent answers inside the same organization. What have you done so far? Who’s driving this, and who just signed off on it? If leadership is pushing AI initiatives from the top down without knowing why, those initiatives are going to keep failing, and it won’t be the tool to blame. The “easy button” myth, and its mirror image on the vendor side RICH: I see this from both sides now that I’ve moved to the vendor side. Too many buyers treat these tools as an “easy button.” They’re not thinking about the time it takes to implement and deploy them, and especially the time it takes to get lawyers to change how they work. From the vendor’s side, there’s a mirror-image problem: a feeling that adoption should be a “no-brainer.” So hesitation reads as friction, not a real concern

blogs.content: A few weeks ago, I spoke on a panel about how to get on a board and what it takes to stay there. It was the last session on the last day of the conference, when most attendees had already left for the airport, but my room was full. That full room told me people want to lead. They have skills and passion, and they want to give back to the communities that have given them so much. Many of them haven’t found where to put that energy yet. In our latest member survey, nearly 9 in 10 members said they want to help shape CLOC, and nearly 30% want a volunteer leadership role. This month, CLOC is giving them that place with the largest volunteer recruitment in our history. More seats at the table than ever before From today through October 31, CLOC is accepting applications for councils, committees and group leadership roles, plus nominations for three open Board seats. We have never offered this many opportunities at once. Three of the councils are new. The first is the Technology & Innovation Council, because AI is moving fast and no one has perfected it, whatever some may claim. Our more than 6,500 members deserve trusted guidance on how AI can benefit them and which red flags to watch for. We’re also building the Professional Advancement & Leadership Development Council because of a question I hear all the time: “Laura, how did you get here?” People want to know which courses to take and who to have coffee with. I expect to join that council myself. The third, the Global Advisory Council, will bring what members see in their own legal markets into CLOC’s plans. We also don’t have all the answers, and I love that. If you see a need among our members, tell us. Some of the best ideas for CLOC’s future will come from the people who raise their hands this month. We’re listening. Who should apply We want applications from across our ecosystem: law firms, in-house teams, academia, government, students and every industry we support. We want senior leaders and people just starting out. If you’re curious, that’s enough to apply. If you’re thinking, “I don’t have enough experience to contribute,” let me tell you a story. A while back, a young student told me she didn’t think she had enough wisdom to share with our Inclusion & Social Impact Council. I told her, “Can you just get in here, please? Let’s figure this out.” She joined, and she told us about the financial hurdles that kept people from attending the CLOC Global Institute (CGI). Her story led us to set aside funding to help people attend the event, and that funding became our Community Access Program (CAP). At CGI this year, so many recipients came up to me, thanking me for the chance to be in this space, and it all started with one student who raised her hand. blogs.author: marcela.valencia@cloc.org
blogs.description: Ten years ago, legal operations wasn’t a job title most people could define with confidence — including, often, the people doing the job. CLOC is now building something that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: a formal certification for legal operations professionals, the Legal Operations Certified Professional (LOCP). As a board member and liaison […] The post Why Legal Operations Is Finally Getting Its Own Credential, And Why That’s Overdue appeared first on CLOC .
blogs.content: Ten years ago, legal operations wasn’t a job title most people could define with confidence — including, often, the people doing the job. CLOC is now building something that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: a formal certification for legal operations professionals, the Legal Operations Certified Professional ( LOCP ) . As a board member and liaison to the advisory committee overseeing this effort, I want to explain why we’re doing this now, how it’s taking shape, and why it matters to how legal departments run. A Profession That’s Outgrown its Own Definition Problem Anyone who has worked in legal ops knows the challenge: the role looks completely different depending on where you sit. A team of one supporting a mid-size company’s legal department has a different day-to-day than someone overseeing a department of 50 or more inside a global enterprise. That variability, among others, has made legal ops notoriously hard to define, and even harder to measure or hire for with confidence. When I started in legal operations, CLOC was about five years old and my GC at the time was looking to transform the legal department, and “legal operations” was the pathway to help operationalize his initiative. But when I discussed my role as a team of one with other legal operations professionals across the country, what I did, I discovered, was different from others in larger corporations. What was consistent among all legal operations professionals are the skills required in order to perform the work. That’s the gap this credential aims to close. The foundation is the CLOC Core 12 , the competency framework CLOC introduced to define what a legal operations professional does, regardless of company size, industry, or where that person sits organizationally. The LOCP will be grounded in the Core 12, so candidates have a real, defined standard to work toward. Earning your LOCP will mean demonstrating your judgment against real scenarios. We’re building the assessment now through a formal job task analysis and standard-setting process, working with practitioners across the field to make sure it reflects the work as it’s done. The goal is to have the first candidates begin that process at CGI in Las Vegas in May 2027. Independent Expertise, Built in From the Start We’ve brought in KaWest Partners and Assessment Systems Corporation, certification and psychometric specialists who’ve built credential programs for other professions, to guide the job task analysis, standard-setting, and validation work now underway alongside our Certification Advisory Committee. Having the best team of specialists in the certification space ensures that this certification means something to not only the examinees but to employers and the overall profession as a whole. Over time, governance of the certification will transition to an independent Certification Board, separate from CLOC’s own Board of Directors, the same kind of separation programs like the PMP or CAE rely on to protect against bias in how standards are set and exams are scored. Ethics and AI as core competencies Ethics isn’t an afterthought here. Whether inside a law firm, in-house, or inside legal tech companies, lawyers operate under model rules of professional responsibility, and legal ops professionals working alongside them need that same grounding. AI is the harder one, because it won’t hold still long enough to test. Capturing it in a static exam is akin to chasing a cat; it doesn’t sit still. So we won’t try to freeze a snapshot of today’s tools into the test. AI sits inside the broader legal tech competency, and the credential itself will be designed to evolve as the technology and the skills required around it shift, with regular recalibration of exam content over time. Subagents Claude spawns in interactive sessions, apart from the ones an agent-team teammate spawns, also run in the background by default. Start a fork yourself with a task that needs everything you’ve discussed so far: Claude Code > /subtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far The fork appears in the panel below your prompt and its result arrives in your conversation when it finishes. Claude discovers your other sessions with the ListAgents tool and sends with SendMessage , either when you ask it to or on its own, such as after a change in one session affects what another is working on. A message is text Claude writes for the other session, never your conversation history or files. Available on macOS and Linux. Requires v2.1.224 or later. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.214 → v2.1.219 3 features · July 20–24 Claude Opus 5 new model Claude Opus 5 is the new default Opus model in Claude Code. It’s the default on Max, Team Premium, Enterprise pay-as-you-go, and the Anthropic API, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform. On the Anthropic API and on Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, Opus 5 runs with a 1M-token context window ; on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, select the 1M model variant. Fast mode moves to Opus 5 at $10/$50 per MTok. Requires v2.1.219 or later. Ask Claude to run or test your app, and the pane opens when the app launches: Claude Code > Build the app and run it in the simulator to check the onboarding flow. Scan a whole repository or only a branch’s diff, a pull request, or a single commit, then turn the findings you choose into reviewed patches that you apply yourself. What's changed

  • Added rows to a mod's Input: a text field of several lines in the terminal, where Enter submits and Shift+Enter or a backslash before Enter starts a new line
  • Added classifier_verdict and permission_mode to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, so auto mode classifier decisions can be told apart from permission rules
  • Added classifier_category to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, naming the built-in rule a classifier block matched, when OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1
  • Fixed quitting removing a worktree made by a WorktreeCreate hook without asking when it may hold unpushed commits
  • Fixed the fable (and best) model alias erroring on the Anthropic API when the newest Fable model is not available to your organization: Claude Code now retries once on the previous Fable model

  • Fixed workflow agents sometimes skipping their step, and the run still reporting success, after reading the harness note that their task text carries no user authority

  • Fixed skills and commands with very many or very long argument names stalling for seconds when invoked; only the first 64 names, each up to 64 characters, are now filled in
  • Fixed skills, commands and hooks using very large amounts of memory when their arguments fill many placeholders
  • Fixed stray characters such as >0q covering the folder trust prompt, and >4m before the shell prompt at exit, in terminals built on VTE older than 0.53 such as MATE Terminal on RHEL 8
  • Fixed stray GOK text appearing in the prompt at startup in some versions of iTerm2

  • Fixed sign-in refresh timeouts and unexpected sign-outs after a short command such as claude auth status or claude plugin list exited in the middle of a token refresh
  • Fixed a tool call cut off by a message sent mid-turn during its permission check being reported to the model as rejected by the user
  • Fixed a case where switching to a model with a smaller context window could spend usage credits on a summary by the previous model without asking first
  • Fixed conversations being compacted over and over, on a model you didn't pick, behind an LLM gateway whose responses name a different model than the one requested
  • Fixed vim mode sometimes staying in INSERT after Escape on a slow or busy machine
  • Fixed Esc discarding a typed AskUserQuestion answer in vim mode: the free-text field now supports vim NORMAL mode, and Esc cancels only from NORMAL
  • Fixed the Read tool reading binary files such as .xlsm, .parquet, .e

blogs.content: What's New Week 24 · June 8–12, 2026 Copy page Copy page Move a session to a new directory with /cd, let subagents spawn their own subagents, and troubleshoot a broken configuration with safe mode. Copy page Copy page Releases v2.1.166 → v2.1.176 3 features · June 8–12 Move a session with /cd v2.1.169 The new /cd command moves the current session to a different working directory without rebuilding the prompt cache: the new directory’s CLAUDE.md is appended as a message instead of replacing the system prompt. The session relocates to the new directory’s project storage, so --resume and --continue find it there. Claude prompts you to trust the directory if you haven’t worked in it before. Move the session into another project without restarting: Claude Code > /cd ../other-project Commands reference Subagents can spawn subagents v2.1.172 Subagents can now spawn their own subagents. The subagent panel below the prompt shows the full tree: each row carries a count of its descendants and a path back to main . Subagent chains are capped at five levels deep to prevent runaway concurrent trees. Open the agents view to watch the nested tree as work fans out: Claude Code > /agents Spawn nested subagents Troubleshoot with safe mode v2.1.169 Start Claude Code with --safe-mode , or set CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE , to launch with all customizations disabled: CLAUDE.md , skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, and custom commands and agents do not load. blogs.description: We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program (CVP), which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals.
blogs.content: Announcements Expanding the Cyber Verification Program Oct 6, 2026 We’re launching a new, expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program (CVP), which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. The program now consists of three access tiers, which allow security teams to apply for the level of access that best suits their work. Each tier includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and new models moving forward. Interested customers can apply here . Cybersecurity is inherently dual use: the same capabilities that enable a security team to find and fix a vulnerability can also help a malicious actor exploit it. For this reason, our generally available models, such as Claude Opus 5.5 , Claude Fable 5.1 , and Claude Sonnet 5.5 , have conservative cyber safeguards that block most cyber work. This is intended to limit the harmful activities malicious actors can carry out using our models, while we continue to work to reduce false positives for secure coding. But defenders also need access to the best tools and most powerful capabilities to secure their systems. For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP . The former gave a group of organizations securing the most critical software access to Claude Mythos; the latter gave vetted security teams access to reduced safeguards on Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet models. Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems. New access tiers The updated access tiers make specific model capabilities available to security professionals based on the scope of their cyber work. Each has different verification requirements and security controls. Defense Access is for defensive work, including security operations center and incident response tasks, reverse-engineering malware, and analyzing and validating vulnerabilities. Examples of qualifying organizations include security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government bodies who are defending systems they own or maintain; operators of critical infrastructure of any size, such as regional hospitals or municipal utilities; smaller security firms; open-source maintainers; and individual researchers with a track record of reported vulnerabilities. We expect many organizations conducting defensive cybersecurity work to qualify for this tier. We aim to respond to applications within a few days. Red Team Access adds authorized penetration testing and red-teaming to the defensive uses above. Examples of qualifying organizations include in-house red teams, government red teams, and security and penetration testing firms. Organizations in this tier can only perform adversarial testing against systems they are authorized to test, including IT systems in critical industries. Users will still experience real-time blocks on actions that could cause physical harm or mass disruption, such as deploying ransomware, damaging physical systems, or pen testing high-risk safety systems. Given the increased eligibility requirements and security controls, we expect applications in this tier to take a few weeks to review. Qualifying organizations will be enrolled in the Defense Access tier while we review their Red Team Access applications. Currently, this tier is for organizations only; individual researchers are not eligible. Specialized Access , which has the fewest cyber blocks, is reserved for a limited set of verified organizations that are authorized to test safety systems that could impact people’s lives or disrupt markets, such as flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure, and government administrative networks. blogs.description: Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.
blogs.content: Policy Preparing for the 2026 US midterms Oct 14, 2026 Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards , which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information. Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms. How people use Claude for elections and politics Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period. 1 Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to increase . This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations. 2 How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for. Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using a privacy-preserving method . Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies. What people ask Claude for in political conversations. Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through Anthropic Insights . Connecting people to trusted sources Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from Democracy Works . Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources. Official voting information presented by Democracy Works. Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation. blogs.content: Announcements Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore Oct 14, 2026 Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI. “We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.” “Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.” Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. blogs.description: We’re publishing a new version of our Usage Policy. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.
blogs.content: Announcements 2026 Usage Policy update Oct 8, 2026 Each year, Anthropic updates its Usage Policy in response to the evolving capabilities of our models, and the feedback we’ve received from our customers. We're publishing a new version of the policy today. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made. Most of the updates in the latest version are intended to clarify existing rules. In the year since our last refresh, Claude has taken on longer, more independent work. This update provides new examples that show how our rules apply to Claude’s new capabilities. It draws on new patterns of misuse in influence operations, weapons development, and surveillance that we’ve observed in the past year (as we’ve documented in our latest threat intelligence report ). We’ve also made updates to clarify our requirements for high-risk use cases in areas like health and finance, to add controls for when Claude is used to autonomously take physical actions, and to address abusive behavior toward our models. The updated policy takes effect on November 12. The full Usage Policy and Supported Regions Policy can be found on their respective pages. A new section on deceptive activity As we wrote about last month , we’ve seen examples of state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial firms using Claude to run networks of fake accounts and fabricated news sites. Our policy already prohibited this activity, but the restrictions were scattered across our elections, fraud, privacy, and disinformation sections. We've consolidated those rules into a new section titled Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity, which applies to deceptive activity of any kind (whether political or commercial). It covers efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts, along with building the tools and infrastructure for running influence operation campaigns. Refocusing our elections section We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. In this version, we’ve further sharpened our section on elections, focusing it specifically on disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections (for instance, by spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout). We’ve renamed it Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes to reflect that scope. For a similar reason, we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting. This prohibition covered legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits using Claude to write information for voters in other languages, or election officials sending ballot cure notices. The behaviors that motivated the original rule (like voter targeting that relies on deception or the misuse of voters’ personal data) remain prohibited under our deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and privacy sections. Clarifying our weapons prohibitions Our Usage Policy has always prohibited using Claude to develop weapons. Recently, we’ve seen people attempt to use our models to build guidance and control software for weapons. The updated section makes clear that our prohibitions include the software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles. These changes reflect how we’ve enforced our previous policy. More precise language on surveillance and law enforcement Our September threat intelligence report documented the growing use of AI to build surveillance systems that identify and track political dissidents. We’ve rewritten our surveillance and criminal justice section to state more precisely what we prohibit.
